full_judgment: 70. The oft-quoted adage 'the King can do no wrong' is the position in England, and her servants, by analogy cannot be sued for tortious liability, but in our country this adage is not applicable to understand the meaning of article 51 of the Constitution. Even our President is not the Executive Head, which vest in the office of Prime Minister alone under article 55 thereof. It may sound a bit off the subject that in India executive power is vested in the President under article 53 of her Constitution. He is a titular head nevertheless. In England it was the Magna Carta that made the monarch titular head. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Pakistan through the Secretary, Ministry of Railways and Communications, Karachi Vs. Muhammad A. Hayat 14 DLR (SC) 7 explained that the constitutional status of the Crown wholly, different from that the Government of Pakistan. The Crown of England occupies a unique position. As stated in Dicey's Law of the Constitution (p. 527 of the 1950 Edition), it is fundamental rule of English Law that no action can be brought against the Crown. No process of any kind can he used by the Courts against the Crown. Another recognized principle is that The Crown can do no wrong. The Crown is not responsible fin its act to anybody or authority and no legal right can be said to exist in any person against the Crown." (emphasis supplied)
